text: In Kuwait, both individuals and society engage in discussions about defense, infrastructure, and cultural differences, expressing frustration and seeking change with the goal of understanding, adapting, and improving their country. These discussions involve various recipients, including government officials, foreigners, and other cultural groups, who receive insights and share their problems in return. This behavior is influenced by Kuwait's multicultural environment and is accompanied by a strong emphasis on beauty standards and social expectations. A significant portion of the sampled population regards this behavior as common, reflecting a normative practice within Kuwaiti society.

In the context of Gulf states and their relations with the West, it is common for the Gulf states to engage in oil trade, attract foreigners, and establish regional unions as part of their economic, social, and political interactions with the West. The primary goals behind these behaviors are to reap economic benefits from oil trade, attract foreigners to contribute to the multicultural fabric of the Gulf states, and achieve political integration through regional unions. Foreigners and the West reciprocate by purchasing oil, residing in the Gulf states, and participating in open border arrangements. The prevalence of these behaviors is widely regarded as normative within the sampled population, reflecting the significant influence and acceptance of these practices in the cultural dynamics of the Gulf states.

In both Kuwait and abroad, individuals from the Kuwaiti cultural group commonly engage in various forms of cultural expression, such as using colloquial language, experiencing culture shock, and interacting with other cultures. This expression is often associated with elements of Americana and can lead to instances of mistaken identity in Europe. The sampled population widely regards this behavior as normative, indicating that the majority of individuals within the Kuwaiti cultural group engage in these cultural expressions both domestically and internationally.

Many Kuwaitis have been educated in the or in Europe so when it comes to communicating with Westerners t hey can be direct and to the point and usually do not beat around the bush. That being said, most Kuwaitis tend to not want to disappoint people in person so they will usually avoid you or give you the run around as opposed to telling you no, I cannot do this or that. Confronting someone or showing anger in public is usually frowned upon as saving face and maintaining a sense of harmony is highly valued.

T he appropriate amount of personal space depends on your sex and the person you are speaking to. Men to men: normally an arms length but it depends on how well the people know each other . Friends and family tend to stand much closer. Men to women: Again, depending on the extreme on one’s religious views, arms length is usually considered most appropriate . Women to men: An a rm’s length or more is appropriate. Women to women: Arm’s length is appropriate but with Westerners they tend to want to stand very close . In the business world there should be no touching during communication. When interacting with friends, one should be very careful and gauge how much touching is allowed based on how much touching the Kuwaiti is using while speaking. There tends to be limited touching between genders when in public.

Eye contact is acceptable but the only issue comes between men and women. As a foreigner, one will want to gauge how much eye contact is acceptable based on whom they are interacting with. Foreign women interacting with local men should be aware that m e n may not look at them even if even if they use direct eye contact. Foreign men interacting with local women will need to be a bit more careful and mirror the level of eye contact being used by the woman.

As a foreigner, you will always be expected to be on time and maybe even a few minutes early. Do not, however, expect the Kuwaitis to be on time. It’s may not seem fair because you could be waiting around for a while but making a Kuwaiti wait on you is a very bad impression to give them.

Most Kuwaiti women are typically in an abaya(body covering) and hijab (head scarf). The more progressive women will just wear figure concealing clothes and nothing over their hair. As a foreigner, you are not expected to cover your hair but may get some odd looks, especially if blonde. In the business world it is important to remain covered as much as possible in western dress.
Head nods in a general direction are commonly used in place of pointing.

Showing the bottoms of your shoes or feet or moving/passing objects with your feet is considered very rude. A ny sort of hostile looking arm movements, especially when driving , are to be avoided . Avoid smoking, eating or drinking in public places during the time of Ramadan. It is considered disrespectful to give or accept anything with your left hand. Strong p ublic displays of affection between genders tend to be culturally inappropriate and offensive.

Alcohol is illegal and it is highly enforced. Upon leaving the airport everyone’s luggage is scanned for alcohol and any found will be confiscated and you do run the risk of being punished. Anyone found with illegal drugs in the country is severely punished. There are rules against public displays of affection as well as pork being allowed in the country.
It is important to be aware of your environment and how people are reacting to you. One must mirror and acclimate oneself to the behavior of those around.

For Men - A b usiness suit is common in most situations. Conservative yet stylish is a good way to go. Darker colors tend to be the norm. For Women - Business suits (pant suit or skirt suit) are common. M ake sure ( as long as it isn’t too hot ) to wear panty hose with the skirt or at the very least that the skirt is more than knee- length. Avoid wearing overly expensive accessories, low necklines and sleeveless attire.

Most people do have titles so take note of their business card and refer to them as such. In the first few minutes of meeting someone, it is customary to exchange business cards. They are generally presented with the right hand but if there is a table or desk between the two people, then it is more common to put the card on the table and slide it across to the person one is meeting with.

It’s best to s how up a few minutes early to meetings . Greet the closest person to you and just take note of the set-up of the meeting. If you do not know who the “boss” is or who is the most important person in the room, then greet everyone with the same level of respect. Small talk is usually expected and as a foreigner, most people are interested to hear about your experiences in country. NEVER say anything negative about the country, even if they do. 5 to 10 minutes of small talk is sufficient and this time can be used to exchange business cards and get a gauge on who the most important person in the room is. As a visitor, even if the people you are meeting do not prompt you to, you may be expected to begin the business discussion and end it. However, the meeting will end when the most important person you are meeting with (sheikh, CEO, President, GM, etc) stands up and shows you out. Meetings do not tend to follow set schedules. Frequent interruptions are common. It's best to just go with the flow. In a business meeting you may be asked your opinion on certain things not pertaining to the business at hand. The best advice give is if asked your opinion on something (for example the elections in the ) then turn the question around and ask whoever initiated the question their opinion. People tend to become defensive and will quickly shut down if they feel you have opposing opinions. It is better to play it safe and figure out what their opinion is so as not to offend them.

Negotiating in is never the same as each person is different. One must remain calm in negotiations but sometimes people may expect you to get a little emotional and pushy with them. Stay polite and respectful but realize that sometimes it is better to be emotional, because people may appreciate it, yet other times they lose respect for you. Just try each in small doses with each person you meet and figure out what works for them. Most decisions are made from the top down and typically take awhile.

Gifts are not expected but if you are going into a long-term partnership with someone or you feel as though someone has helped you and you would like to thank them, then by all means, gifts are allowed. Gifts are normally opened in private with a thank you being sent after. If you are given a gift, unless prompted otherwise, you do not open it until you leave and a thank you e-mail is expected. Pretty much any standard gift you would give for business is appropriate. Alcohol is inappropriate as would be anything not in line with Islam.

Unacceptable attire would be anything too revealing or shapely. Avoid tank-tops, shorts, ripped jeans, etc. It is important to understand that although a foreigner is not expected to dress in the traditional garb of the gulf, that a certain amount of intelligence and understanding must be used when selecting clothing to wear in this conservative country.

Most students socialize by attending what are known as diwaniyas. These are separate rooms for socializing that were traditionally used for men on a weekly basis to discuss politics. They have been adopted by the youth to hang out with friends, watch movies, play video games, etc. There are parties to attend but the most common forms of socializing amongst the youth are smoking sheesha(hookah/water-pipe), going out to dinner at one of the many restaurants, or going to the mall and/or movies. Drinking is illegal, but smoking is accepted. More so for men than women. There are strict social standards for interaction between men and women and when/if it comes to dating, men do the majority of the asking. Typical dates when/if they happen, include going to the movies and/or going to dinner.

국제기구 가입 현황 021 Ⅴ Ⅵ 경제 기타 사회 문화 1. 왕위 계승 방식 헌법 제4조는 쿠웨이트 국왕은 무바라크 대제의 후손 중에서만 선택할 수 있도록 규정 왕위를 승계하는 왕세자(Crown Prince)는 알 사바 왕가 대표자 회의에서 다수결 투표 형식으로 선정하며 의회의 동의 절차를 거쳐 국왕이 즉위 1년 이내 임명 - 국왕이 지명한 왕세자가 의회 인준에 실패할 경우, 국왕이 추천한 3명 이상의 복수 후보 중에서 의회가 왕세자를 결정(헌법 제4조) 제7대 국왕인 무바라크 사후 형제인 자베르 국왕과 살림 국왕이 왕위를 연이어 계승한 이후 두 국왕의 후계인 자베르 가문과 살림 가문이 교대로 왕위를 승계하는 것이 전통 나.

알 사바 왕가의 경제 참여에 대한 재계 가문과의 알력 쿠웨이트는 1752년 성립 당시부터 지배 가문 간의 역할 분담이 이루어져, 알 사바 가문은 통치와 군사적 역할을, 현(現) 바레인 왕가인 알 칼리파 가문은 국내 교역을, 알 잘라히마 가문 등은 해외무역 등을 담당 그러나 석유 생산이 쿠웨이트의 주 산업이 된 이후, 알 사바 왕가가 석유업을 바탕으로 부를 축적하여 경제적 역할을 확대하고, 정부에서 추진하는 경제개혁, 개방정책 등이 기존 재계 가문들의 전통적 경제적 이권에 영향을 미치자 자주 갈등이 발생하고 있으며 의회 내 정치적 대립으로도 발전 다.

8월 전원 체포) 등 일련의 사건으로 매년 대테러 활동을 강화 중 - 압달리 사건 등에서 국왕의 리더십하에 쿠웨이트 국민이 단합하고 연대하는 모습을 보임으로써 쿠웨이트 내에서 종파 간의 갈등을 부채질하기 위한 IS의 시도는 실패 ※ 쿠웨이트인 중 시아파가 1/3을 차지하고 있으며 사우디나 바레인 시아파에 비해 상대적으로 차별대우를 덜 받고 있어 1980년대를 제외하고는 쿠웨이트 내에서 종파 간 갈등이 거의 발생하지 않았으나 2011년 바레인에서 종파 간 갈등이 재연된 후 IS 세력은 종파 간 갈등을 부채질하기 위해 시아파 사원에 폭탄테러 자행 72 STATE OF KUWAIT 쿠 웨이트 정부는 2015.

교육 교류 한 국 학생의 쿠웨이트 파견 - 쿠웨이트 고등교육부 주관으로 쿠웨이트 대학에서 실시하는 1년간의 아랍어 어학 과정(학비 무상 및 생활비 지원)에 매년 우리 학생 10명이 참여하여 아랍어 연수를 받고 있으며, 2015년부터는 한국 학생 선발 인원이 8명에서 매년 10명으로 증원 쿠 웨이트 학부 과정 매년 한국인 장학생 입학 - 2015년부터 쿠웨이트 대학교 인문대학 학부과정에 한국인 장학생 쿼터 1명이 신설되었으며, 현재 한국인 학생 1명이 신문방송학 전공 과정에 재학 중 쿠 웨이트 내 한국어 진흥을 위한 세종학당 운영 - 한국의 K-Culture가 쿠웨이트 내에서도 선풍적인 인기를 누리면서 “한국어 학습”에 대한 인지도 또한 계속 상승하는 분위기를 반영하여, 2023.

의복 여 름이 매우 길고 겨울이 짧은 계절적 특성이 있으나 여름철에는 극단 적인 고온으로 냉방시설이 완비된 실내에서 주로 생활하는 점을 감안, 오히려 긴팔, 긴바지 등 한국의 춘추복 필요 겨울은 가장 추운 경우에도 한국의 늦가을 또는 초겨울 날씨에 불과 하므로 아주 두꺼운 한겨울용 의류보다는 스웨터, 트렌치코트, 얇은 점퍼류 등이 유용하며, 난방시설이 없는 경우가 대다수이므로 전기담요 등이 유용 태 양광선이 강하고 자외선지수가 높아 선글라스 착용이 필수적 전통의상을 착용한 미샬 국왕 전통의상을 만화로 표현 전통의상을 착용한 여성의 모습 152 STATE OF KUWAIT 5.

TIP 제도 쿠 웨이트 일상생활에서 팁 문화의 전통이 강하게 있는 편은 아니나, 쿠웨이트 내 서비스업에 종사하는 외국인 노동자들은 선진국 국민에 대해서는 팁을 기대하는 분위기가 있기 때문에, 쇼핑몰 직원이 구입 물품을 차량까지 운반해 주는 경우 등 만족한 서비스를 제공받은 경우 개인 판단하에 팁(250fils~1KD) 제공 가능 다. 애비뉴 몰 명 칭: Avenues Mall 위 치: 슈와이크, 5번 링 로드 자하라 방향 건 축 구조 및 특징 - 2007년 개장 이래 지속적으로 개발하고 있는 쿠웨이트 최대의 쇼핑몰이자 쿠웨 이트를 대표하는 랜드마크 - 애비뉴몰에는 명품관, 실내전통시장, IKEA, 11개 스크린을 보유한 대형 영화관, 하이퍼 슈퍼마켓인 카르푸, 스파숍, 어린이 놀이시설 등과 총 800개 이상의 상점과 식당이 존재 애비뉴 몰 내부 178 STATE OF KUWAIT 마.

무바라키야 전통시장 명 칭: Souk Al Mubarakiya 위 치: 쿠웨이트시티 특 징 - 이 시장은 최소 200년 이상의 역사가 있는 가장 오래된 시장(Souk) 중 하나이며, 석유 발견 이전 대표적인 무역 중심지 - 1990년 이라크 침공 당시 대부분이 손상되었으나 종전 후 복원 작업을 통해 전통 적인 멋을 유지한 쿠웨이트를 대표하는 전통시장으로 부활 - 취급 물품: 페르시아 실크 카펫, 아랍 골동품, 전통의상, 스카프, 수제 향수, 금, 은, 보석, 꿀, 향신료, 과자, 야채, 과일, 고기, 생선, 대추야자 등 무바라키야 전통시장 모습 180 STATE OF KUWAIT 사.
